front: What RAM form factor do laptops use?
back: SODIMM (Small Outline DIMM) — physically shorter than desktop DIMMs. DDR4 SODIMMs have 260 pins, DDR5 SODIMMs have 262.

front: Compare TN, IPS, and VA LCD panel types.
back: TN: fastest response, cheapest, worst color/viewing angles. IPS: best color accuracy and viewing angles, slower response. VA: best contrast, middle ground on the rest.

front: What advantage does OLED have over LCD?
back: Each pixel emits its own light, so blacks are true black (pixel off), contrast is effectively infinite, and no backlight is needed — thinner panels, better power efficiency on dark content.

front: What is a digitizer in a mobile device display?
back: The layer that converts touch/stylus input into digital signals the OS can use. A cracked glass with working touch = digitizer intact; touch dead with intact image = digitizer failed.

front: Difference between USB tethering and a mobile hotspot?
back: Both share the phone's cellular data. Tethering shares it over a USB cable to one device; a hotspot broadcasts Wi-Fi so multiple devices can connect.

front: Name the three common mobile device connectors.
back: USB-C (reversible, current standard), Lightning (Apple proprietary, pre-USB-C iPhones), micro-USB (older Android/accessories).

front: What does airplane mode do?
back: Disables all radios: cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and NFC. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can usually be re-enabled individually while cellular stays off.

front: What is NFC and what is it used for?
back: Near-Field Communication — very short range (~4 cm) radio. Used for contactless payments (Apple Pay/Google Pay), transit cards, and quick device pairing.

front: What does DHCP do, and what are the four steps of a lease?
back: Automatically assigns IP configuration (address, mask, gateway, DNS). DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

front: What does DNS do?
back: Resolves human-readable names (example.com) to IP addresses. Key records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), MX (mail), CNAME (alias), TXT (verification/SPF).

front: A device has the address 169.254.20.7. What does that tell you?
back: It's an APIPA/link-local address — the client failed to reach a DHCP server and self-assigned. It can only talk to the local segment. Investigate DHCP or the connection.

front: Router vs switch vs access point — one-line roles.
back: Router: forwards traffic between networks (and to the internet). Switch: connects wired devices within a LAN using MAC addresses. AP: bridges wireless clients onto the wired LAN.

front: 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz Wi-Fi trade-offs?
back: 2.4 GHz: longer range, better wall penetration, only 3 non-overlapping channels (1/6/11), crowded. 5 GHz: faster, many more channels, less interference, shorter range.

front: What is a VLAN?
back: A virtual LAN — logically segments one physical switch into multiple isolated broadcast domains (e.g., voice vs data, guest vs corporate) without separate hardware.

front: What is a VPN?
back: An encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network (usually the internet) that makes a remote device appear to be on the private network. Protects traffic on public Wi-Fi and enables remote access to internal resources.

front: TCP vs UDP?
back: TCP: connection-oriented, three-way handshake, guaranteed ordered delivery (web, email, file transfer). UDP: connectionless, no delivery guarantee, lower overhead (streaming, VoIP, DNS queries, gaming).

front: DDR4 vs DDR5 — key differences?
back: DDR5: higher data rates (4800 MT/s+ vs DDR4's typical 2133–3200), lower voltage (1.1 V vs 1.2 V), on-module power management (PMIC), two independent 32-bit subchannels per module. Slots are not compatible.

front: What is ECC RAM and where is it used?
back: Error-Correcting Code memory — detects and corrects single-bit memory errors on the fly. Used in servers and workstations where silent data corruption is unacceptable. Requires motherboard/CPU support.

front: Max throughput of SATA III?
back: 6 Gb/s (about 600 MB/s usable). This is why SATA SSDs plateau around 550 MB/s regardless of brand.

front: What is NVMe and why is it faster than SATA?
back: Non-Volatile Memory Express — a protocol that lets SSDs talk directly over PCIe lanes instead of the SATA bus, with far deeper command queues. Gen4 x4 drives reach ~7,000 MB/s vs SATA's ~550 MB/s.

front: What is M.2?
back: A compact expansion form factor (a slot on the board, no cables). Common size 2280 = 22 mm wide, 80 mm long. An M.2 slot can carry SATA or NVMe/PCIe signals — the drive and slot keying must match.

front: RAID 0, 1, 5, 10 in one line each.
back: 0: striping, speed, no redundancy — one disk dies, all data lost. 1: mirroring, survives one disk. 5: striping + parity (min 3 disks), survives one disk. 10: mirrored stripes (min 4), fast + survives one disk per mirror pair.

front: LGA vs PGA CPU sockets?
back: LGA (Land Grid Array): pins in the socket, flat pads on the CPU — modern Intel and AMD AM5. PGA (Pin Grid Array): pins on the CPU — AMD through AM4.

front: What is a TPM?
back: Trusted Platform Module — a dedicated crypto chip (or firmware equivalent) that stores keys and platform measurements. Backs BitLocker drive encryption, Secure Boot attestation, and Windows 11's hardware requirement.

front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS?
back: IaaS: provider gives you VMs/storage/network, you manage OS and up (EC2). PaaS: provider manages runtime, you deploy code (Heroku, App Service). SaaS: finished application you just use (Microsoft 365, Gmail).

front: Public vs private vs hybrid cloud?
back: Public: shared provider infrastructure (AWS/Azure/GCP). Private: dedicated to one organization, on-prem or hosted. Hybrid: both connected, workloads move between them.

front: Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisor?
back: Type 1 (bare metal): runs directly on hardware — ESXi, Hyper-V, Proxmox. Type 2 (hosted): runs as an app on a normal OS — VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.

front: VM vs container?
back: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS per instance. Containers share the host kernel and isolate at the process level — much lighter, faster to start, but same-OS only.

front: What is rapid elasticity in cloud computing?
back: Capacity scales up and down automatically with demand — you get more instances during a spike and shed them after, paying only for what ran.

front: What is metered utilization?
back: Pay-as-you-go: the provider measures exactly what you consume (compute-hours, GB stored, requests) and bills on that measurement rather than a flat fee.

front: What is VDI?
back: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure — users' desktop OSes run as VMs in the data center/cloud, streamed to thin clients. Centralizes data and management; the endpoint holds nothing.

front: Why use a VM as a sandbox or test environment?
back: Snapshots and isolation: you can detonate suspicious files or test risky changes, then roll back to a clean snapshot in seconds. Nothing touches the host OS.

front: List the six steps of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology.
back: 1) Identify the problem. 2) Establish a theory of probable cause. 3) Test the theory. 4) Establish a plan of action and implement it. 5) Verify full functionality and implement preventive measures. 6) Document findings, actions, and outcomes.

front: What is SMART and what should you do when it warns?
back: Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology — drives track their own health metrics (reallocated sectors, pending sectors). On a SMART warning: back up immediately and plan drive replacement; failure is likely.

front: What is POST and what does a beep code mean?
back: Power-On Self-Test — firmware hardware check before boot. Beep codes (or debug LEDs) signal a failure detected before video initializes: commonly RAM, GPU, or CPU. Codes vary by BIOS vendor — check the board manual.

front: PC powers on (fans spin) but no display. First checks?
back: Monitor power and input source; cable seated at both ends; correct output port (GPU, not motherboard, when a dedicated GPU is installed). Then reseat RAM and GPU, listen for beep codes, try one RAM stick at a time.

front: What do swollen/distended capacitors on a motherboard indicate?
back: Failing capacitors — bulged or leaking tops. Cause random reboots, failure to POST, instability. The board (or PSU, if there) needs replacement; it will only get worse.

front: System shuts down or throttles under load. Likely cause and fixes?
back: Overheating. Check: dust-clogged heatsinks/filters (clean with compressed air), failed or misseated fans, dried-out thermal paste (repaste), blocked airflow, ambient temperature. Verify temps in firmware or monitoring software.

front: Users report intermittent Wi-Fi drops on 2.4 GHz in a dense office. Likely fix?
back: Co-channel interference — neighboring APs overlapping. Move APs to the non-overlapping channels (1, 6, 11), reduce power so cells don't overlap, or move clients to 5 GHz.

front: Laser printer prints with a repeating vertical line/streak. Likely cause?
back: A scratched or dirty imaging drum (or a failing toner cartridge if the drum is integrated). Repeating defects at a fixed interval correspond to one roller's circumference — replace that component.

front: Site-to-site VPN vs client-to-site (remote-access) VPN?
back: Site-to-site: an always-on tunnel between two routers/gateways, joining two whole networks (e.g., branch office to HQ) — transparent to the devices behind each end. Client-to-site: a VPN app on one device connects that single user in, typically for remote/home workers.
